standard.title: Draw conclusions
standard.description: draw conclusions based on the analysis of the data and information
standard.prior_knowledge: Students draw conclusions based on analysis of data (AC9HG7S04). At Y8, conclusions must explicitly draw on geographical concepts (place, space, environment, interconnections, sustainability, scale, change) as organisers.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students draw conclusions from data analysis using at least one geographical concept as an organiser, and explain reasons for decisions and choices.

nodes.label: Geographical concepts as conclusion organisers
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and apply at least one geographical concept (place, space, environment, interconnections, sustainability, scale, change) as an organiser for drawing conclusions.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify one geographical concept and explain how it could organise their conclusions from a data analysis.
nodes.typical_width: Students apply at least one of the geographical concepts of place, space, environment, interconnections, sustainability, scale or change as an organiser to form a conclusion responding to an inquiry question — e.g., using 'interconnections' to conclude about the relationship between landscape value and tourism pressure.
wider: Apply two or more geographical concepts simultaneously, showing how they interact in the conclusion.
Compare how different concept choices (e.g., 'scale' vs 'interconnections') lead to different conclusions from the same data.
Examine what each concept reveals and what it obscures as a conclusion organiser.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without explicitly using a geographical concept as organiser, students' conclusions default to restating data observations rather than geographic explanation. The concept-organiser move is what makes a geographic conclusion distinct from a general summary.

response_modes.reason: Using a geographical concept as a conclusion organiser is a formal disciplinary move that requires explicit instruction. Students need to see the difference between 'the data shows X' and 'this data demonstrates how interconnections between Y and Z explain X'.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The set of seven geographical concepts offers rich analytical flexibility — wider students can explore which concept most powerfully organises their findings and why, building sophisticated disciplinary reasoning.
success_criteria: Names at least one geographical concept and uses it explicitly to organise a conclusion.
Explains how the concept helps make sense of the data analysis findings.

nodes.label: Drawing and explaining conclusions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can draw conclusions that respond to the inquiry question and explain the reasons for their decisions and choices.
nodes.minimum_width: Students draw one conclusion from analysis findings and provide one reason supporting it.
nodes.typical_width: Students draw conclusions from research findings or data analysis — about the impacts of geomorphological hazards or urbanisation on people, places and environments — using at least one geographical concept as an organiser and explaining the reasoning behind significant decisions (e.g., why particular evidence was weighted, why an impact was judged significant).
wider: Develop conclusions that acknowledge counter-evidence or alternative interpretations.
Evaluate the strength of the conclusion relative to the quality and quantity of evidence supporting it.
Reflect on how the choice of geographical concept organiser influenced the conclusion reached.

response_modes.reason: Drawing a conclusion integrates analysis (S03), concept application (Node 1) and explanatory reasoning into a response to the inquiry question — the endpoint of the geographical inquiry cycle.

success_criteria: States a conclusion that directly responds to the inquiry question.
Explains at least one reason for a decision or choice made in reaching the conclusion, citing evidence.
